about: How the country's opinion of its president moves (Nation, Nov 8, 2026). Read by src/core2/modules/national-opinion.ts. Every number is tagged SOURCED, ESTIMATED (with source and spread) or TUNABLE. Disasters carry no weight in approval: Gallup finds 'little evidence' that Hurricane Katrina moved the president's overall job approval (43 percent in August 2005, 44 in September, 41 in October, 38 in November, with the Miers nomination and two indictments in the same months; news.gallup.com/poll/24283/little-impact-katrina-bushs-overall-job-ratings.aspx), so a disaster pushes approval by nothing here and no read is built for it. Sized pushes wait for a producer: a scandal (Iran-Contra, 63 to 47 percent in two months, recovered over about 20; Watergate, 62 to 24 over 21 months; news.gallup.com/poll/4258) or a rally (the Iran hostage crisis, +27 points, back to the start in about 5 months). See pool item nation-federal-scandal-producer.

longRunMeanPct.source: The point where the two parties break even in a vote: approval of 50 percent is neutral for the president's party (the race reads the gap from it, electorate-inputs.ts). The base is not pulled toward it. Coggin, Economics & Politics, 2025, doi 10.1111/ecpo.12322 finds quarterly Gallup approval 1960-2022 stationary around a mean near 50 percent.

openingPct.source: Where the country's approval of the sitting president stands on the first day of play: Gallup's readings for the president in 2025 ran from the high 30s to the low 40s (Gallup, Presidential Job Approval Center). The world then moves it from what happens.

pointsPerUnemploymentPoint.source: Approval points lost per point the unemployment rate rose over the year: studies of presidential approval find about 0.3 to 1 point per point (Mueller, War, Presidents and Public Opinion, 1973; survey of the economic determinants of approval, Leuphana, about half of studies find a significant effect). The base fades slowly (persistence), so the felt effect builds over months.

pointsPerInflationPoint.source: Approval points lost per point annual inflation rose over the year: rising prices and expected price rises consistently lower approval (Coggin, 2025); the size is similar to or smaller than unemployment's (Newman and Ostrom, 2002).
